title: Active spherical wheel: current dynamics, control and estimation

pages.title: Understand the controller, then defend the results
pages.section: Study guide • current selected simulation baseline

blocks.text: Active spherical wheel: dynamics, gain-scheduled LQR, contact-aware feedforward, momentum-based contact estimation and incoming-drive preview. Prepared 26 November 2026 from the current implementation and saved experiment evidence.

The key correction: the actuator bounds already limit the applied commands. A remaining design gap is consistent anticipation of those limits before a large correction is clipped; addressing that gap is not yet a proven drift cure. A penalty on effort is not a hard inequality constraint.
What this guide establishes

items: The 0.835 m/s belt request is mostly balance feedback in one inspected event; the desired body speed there is only about 0.045 m/s. These are different quantities.
Some configurations lose sideways authority because the drive velocity directions align. Small tracking error must sometimes be accepted; cost tuning cannot create a missing direction.
The saved lockstep tests do not demonstrate robot motion during Python computation. Filtering, preceding-interval information, patch boundaries and solver/state timing must be separated.
Turning overshoot is measurable, but previous improvements came with tradeoffs. The selected LQR baseline remains unchanged.

blocks.text: Scope

This is a preparation document, not a five-minute slide deck. It explains the selected loop and re-examines existing logs. No new simulation or controller change was performed for this document. Cameras and deployment questions are outside this presentation scope.

Evidence labels throughout: Implemented = code actually in the selected loop. Observed = saved trace or controlled comparison. Interpretation = explanation consistent with that evidence. Proposed = not an adopted fix.

blocks.text: Three terms to keep separate

rows: Translation of the wheel center in the world, m/s.
Desired shaft/shell angular rate, rad/s, or belt surface speed, m/s.
Three joint torques plus two prescribed belt surface speeds. A joint-rate reference is not itself a torque command.

blocks.text: Also distinguish tracking a timed trajectory from returning to a geometric path, and absolute platform tilt from error relative to its intended lean. Those distinctions change the interpretation of several videos.

pages.title: One complete control interval

blocks.caption: Blue arrows belong to the selected controller. The truth branch is evaluated separately and does not enter the observer-based command calculation.

items: At time t, read current simulated configuration and velocity plus the input applied over the preceding interval.
Update the momentum residual. Locate support patches from its filtered force/moment at the current configuration.
Update the filtered ground normal and load estimate. Build desired body attitude, joint-rate references and holding feedforward.
Compute scheduled LQR feedback. Blend incoming-drive preparation and fade low-load torque. The optional heading helper is disabled in this selected baseline. Clip the final request.
Hold that input for five 1 ms Gazebo/DART physics steps. Read the new state; repeat at 200 Hz on the simulated clock.

blocks.text: The observer estimates; the LQR corrects; feedforward anticipates the motion implied by current geometry. These are distinct parts of the same closed loop.

Selected settings: mode="hardware" is the repository name for the observer-and-locator interface; it is still used here in simulation. rolling_allocation="least_squares"; synchronize=True; tilt_reference=None; heading_gain=0. The generic OffroadParams default is a different contact-reading comparison mode.

pages.title: Coordinates, axes and the five inputs

blocks.text: The mechanism is a floating base (fork/platform), a carrier rotating about the fork’s y axis, and two shells rotating independently about the carrier’s x axis. Belt caps are attached to the carrier. Their surface motion is prescribed at contact rather than represented by additional dynamic belt joints.
q=(x,y,z,Q_w,Q_x,Q_y,Q_z,\theta_s,\theta_A,\theta_B)
v=(v_x,v_y,v_z,\omega_x,\omega_y,\omega_z,\dot\theta_s,\dot\theta_A,\dot\theta_B)

rows: 10 stored values: 3 position + 4 quaternion + 3 joint angles. The quaternion has one unit-norm constraint.
9 independent velocity coordinates. Free-base angular velocity uses the body frame in this model; world force/moment conversion must respect that.
18 values: 9 configuration-tangent errors plus 9 velocity errors. Attitude error is a three-dimensional rotation error, not four quaternion differences.

blocks.text: u=(\tau_s,\tau_A,\tau_B,s_A,s_B)

Sphere radius R=0.12 m. Current total model mass is 1.86 kg. World frame: z is up. Motor torque, angular-rate target and belt surface speed must never be summed or compared without their declared scaling.

pages.sources: [C1] config/model.yaml; [C2] model.py, sim.py; [T4] MuJoCo generalized-coordinate conventions.

pages.title: The forward dynamics actually used

blocks.text: M(q)\dot v+c(q,v)=B_\tau\tau+f_p(q,v)+Q_{\mathrm{ext}}
Q_{\mathrm{ext}}=\sum_i J_i(q)^T f_i

M is the configuration-dependent inertia matrix. c contains gravity and velocity-dependent bias forces. fp contains passive terms such as joint damping. The three joint torques enter through Bτ. Contact forces fi are solved by the physics engine; they act through contact Jacobians Ji.

The recent work changes estimation, reference construction, routing and diagnostics; it does not introduce a new fundamental mass/bias equation. The generated multibody model and its standard dynamic terms remain the basis of the selected controller.
Where do the belts appear?

A belt command changes the target tangential velocity of its contacting surface. The resulting traction enters the solved contact force. It is not an extra generalized torque in B<sub>τ</sub>, and there are no two extra belt inertia states in this model.
What determines contact force?

items: Geometry and separation determine which surfaces can touch.
Normal contact is unilateral: the ground can push on the wheel, but cannot pull it into the ground.
Available tangential traction is friction-limited. A Coulomb cone is a useful conceptual description; the actual Gazebo/DART solver uses its configured discrete contact/friction formulation.
Moving belt surfaces modify the tangential contact condition. If traction is insufficient, commanded surface motion need not become the desired body motion.

blocks.text: The full dynamics are nonlinear and contact-dependent. The LQR is designed from local discrete approximations of this nonlinear step; the Gazebo robot does not evolve according to one fixed A,B matrix.

Gazebo/DART produces the saved trajectories. MuJoCo provides the companion model, local design computations and observer model terms. Solver contact truth is logged for evaluation, separately from the selected controller input.

pages.sources: [C2] model.py/sim.py; [C10] gazebo/plant.py and bridge; [T4] MuJoCo computation; [T6] Gazebo physics documentation.

pages.title: From body velocity to rolling references

blocks.text: A contact point moves because the base translates, the base rotates, the carrier/shell rotates, and possibly the belt surface moves. Ideal rolling asks for zero tangential surface velocity relative to the ground.
P_t\left(v_c+\omega_W\times r+\sum_j\dot\theta_j(a_j\times r)+s\,d\right)=0

r: center-to-contact vector; a<sub>j</sub>: world joint-axis direction; d: world belt travel direction; P<sub>t</sub>=I−nnᵀ: projection onto a local tangent plane. This is a physical explanation, not a claim that the native allocator solves this full equation.
The native allocator’s actual approximation
J_{xy}(q,\hat{r},\widehat{\mathrm{patch}})\,z\simeq- v_{\mathrm{ref},xy}
z=(\dot\theta_s^*,\dot\theta_A^*,\dot\theta_B^*,s_A^*,s_B^*)

The implemented rolling allocator stacks world-horizontal XY contact-Jacobian rows. It computes a minimum normalized-rate least-squares solution. Native rate scales are 5 rad/s for joints and 0.3 m/s for belts: these are normalization preferences, not hard angular-speed limits.

items: The first three allocated values become joint-velocity references. The LQR supplies the torque needed to approach them.
The two belt references also enter directly as rolling feedforward speed commands.
Native least squares uses inferred contact identities/points, but does not numerically weight its rows by load shares. The experimental bounded allocator has a different weighted formulation.

blocks.text: This is a velocity-consistency calculation. It does not prove the allocated motion can be accelerated, balanced or sustained within torque and friction limits.

pages.sources: [C6] experiments.py:_rolling_allocation and rolling_feedforward_records; [C5] command reference construction.

pages.title: How balance and holding references are built

blocks.text: The desired body position comes from the timed path. The desired attitude also responds to the inferred ground normal and requested horizontal acceleration. A balanced platform on a slope may therefore be intentionally tilted relative to vertical.
\ell_{xy}=\frac{a_{\mathrm{ref},xy}}{g}-\kappa\hat{n}_{xy},\qquad \kappa=\frac{m_{\mathrm{total}}R}{m_{\mathrm{upper}}h_{\mathrm{upper}}}

Here ℓ is the horizontal part of the desired up-vector before its magnitude is bounded. The code converts that tilt into a quaternion and combines it with current yaw. The 28° setting caps the requested lean; it is not a proof of allowable terrain slope or actual tilt.
Static holding feedforward
\tau_{s,\mathrm{hold}}=mgR\,[a_s\times\hat{n}]_z
\tau_{A,\mathrm{hold}}=w_A mgR\,[a_h\times\hat{n}]_z,\quad \tau_{B,\mathrm{hold}}=w_B mgR\,[a_h\times\hat{n}]_z

The shell shares w<sub>A</sub>,w<sub>B</sub> route holding torque to inferred shell support. This component does not provide a belt holding torque: belt entries are zero because those channels are surface speeds.
What feedback is intentionally relaxed?

items: The target z is set to the current wheel-center z, suppressing vertical position error rather than pulling the wheel back to one global height. Vertical reference velocity is made consistent with the local plane.
Absolute shell material-angle errors are suppressed. The shaft angle error is tied to rolling position error rather than blindly tracking accumulated angle.
Position and linear-velocity errors are rotated into the current heading frame. Default yaw is free. Yaw-rate feedback can still act through LQR; the separate heading helper is disabled.

blocks.text: A changing lean reference with an insufficient or zero desired angular-rate reference can create substantial attitude/rate demand. That was investigated in I-43; smoothing it improved some metrics but failed the broader comparison.

pages.sources: [C5] lean_vector, reference_attitude, support_torque, _terrain_feedback; [E43].

pages.title: What LQR optimizes and what K means

blocks.text: The local 5 ms nonlinear step is differentiated numerically around a balanced operating point. Perturbing each error coordinate and each input gives the discrete matrices A and B.
e_{k+1}\simeq A e_k+B\,\delta u_k
\mathcal{J}=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\left(\tilde{e}_k^T Q\tilde{e}_k+\tilde{u}_k^T R_u\tilde{u}_k\right)

State and input scales produce dimensionless errors and inputs before the Riccati equation is solved. Input bounds are used as scales in this design. Scaling by a bound is not imposing an inequality. The implementation reduces the local system to its reachable subspace and checks discarded unstable modes.
K=(R_u+B^TPB)^{-1}B^TPA,\qquad \delta u=-Ke

The formula is shown in one consistent coordinate system; the code transforms the normalized/reduced solution back to physical input and error units. It uses SciPy’s discrete algebraic Riccati solver.
Gain scheduling

A precomputed bank supplies local gains at different phases/supports. The scheduled gains are blended using inferred support loads; the selected shaft feedback row is kept from the ordinary local design. Default phase scheduling refers to world vertical, while the inferred normal still affects lean and holding torque.

LQR gives an optimal policy for its declared local, unconstrained quadratic problem. That statement does not certify the full nonlinear, switching, clipped controller globally. We have not established such a certificate.

Normalized effort weights are R<sub>u</sub>=diag(0.3,0.3,0.3,1,1). These weigh the five normalized command channels; they are not electrical power or a measured energy model. Configuration errors live in an 18-dimensional tangent/velocity representation.

pages.title: Why an effort penalty is not a hard constraint

blocks.text: Your concern is correct: command feasibility is a controller-design issue. But the existing clamp is working. The missing feature is anticipation of saturation and its effect on balance/tracking, not the existence of a final numeric limit.
A deliberately simple quadratic example
\min_u\ (x+u)^2+r_u u^2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad u^*=-\frac{x}{1+r_u}

For x=10 and r<sub>u</sub>=1, the unconstrained optimum is u=−5. If the allowed range is [−1,1], the optimum still lies outside it because the optimization never included that range. Adding |u|≤1 changes the problem; clipping afterward changes the action but not the prediction that generated it. This is a one-step teaching example, not a robot test.
Three different “effort/limit” mechanisms in our code

rows: Soft cost on normalized input deviation. It can prefer a large command when predicted state error is costly.
Native least squares chooses normalized drive rates. Experimental bounded/feasible modes have speed/rate inequalities; those modes are inactive in the selected baseline.
Hard-bounds the total issued command after feedback, feedforward and preparation. It guarantees those numeric input bounds, not successful balance or tracking.

blocks.text: Increasing the LQR effort penalty can reduce demand, but generally also weakens correction. A nonzero linear gain can produce an arbitrarily large request for sufficiently large error. A finite penalty therefore cannot enforce a fixed bound for every error.

Native joint-rate and acceleration reference limits are not enforced merely because their settings exist in OffroadParams. Only the active branch applies them. Constraints on references also do not constrain every later feedback addition.

pages.sources: [C3] normalized Q/R design; [C5] branch selection and final np.clip; [C6] native allocation; [T1] constrained versus unconstrained LQR.

pages.title: Where the command changes before application

blocks.text: u_0=u_{\mathrm{eq}}+u_{\mathrm{roll}}+u_{\mathrm{hold}}-K(\phi,\hat{w})e
u_1=(1-\beta)\odot u_0+\beta\odot u_{\mathrm{prepare}}
u_2=u_1+u_{\mathrm{heading}},\qquad u_3=\mathrm{fade}(u_2)
u_{\mathrm{applied},i}=\min(b_i,\max(-b_i,u_{3,i}))

The optional heading term is zero in the selected baseline. The request in a saved “requested” field is the result before final clipping, after the active preparation/heading/fade additions. The shadow routing audit also saves an earlier pre-synchronization command so one change can be isolated. Do not compare these as though they were the same signal.
Why clipping can change the intended behavior

items: Feedback is designed around an approximate relationship between requested input and the next state. Saturation changes that relationship.
One drive may hit its bound before another. Independent clipping can change the direction and relative balance/travel contributions of the combined correction.

References may continue moving while the robot cannot keep up, increasing state error and requesting still more correction. That is not automatically an integral-windup claim; the feedback includes evolving references/history without a generic integral state.

blocks.text: A QP that only minimizes distance to u<sub>request</sub> under independent box bounds can be equivalent to clipping. A meaningful improvement needs dynamic/geometry-aware priorities or feasible references, rather than renaming the same clamp “optimization”.
A feasible controller still cannot guarantee an impossible task. When balance, path motion and bounds conflict, the design must explicitly decide what may relax and when to stop or recover.

pages.title: The saturated event, with numbers

blocks.text: At t=6.825 s in the original Mars figure-eight, the controller correctly selects belt A. Desired horizontal body velocity is approximately (0.03244,0.03128) m/s, a magnitude of 0.0451 m/s. Nevertheless, belt A requests 0.83474 m/s.
Attitude and angular-rate terms account for 88.6% of this LQR contribution. This particular large request is not primarily the rolling feedforward trying to execute a fast path.

Actual absolute tilt is about 7.64° and the reference tilt about 12.03°. The full up-vector error is about 5.29°; subtracting scalar tilt magnitudes is not the same geometric error. The large balance correction occurs before the sustained path departure at 6.860 s.

Holding, preparation, heading, fade and equilibrium contributions to this belt channel are zero at this sample. The exact sums were rechecked from saved gain/error/full-precision arrays. This is one diagnostic sample within a logged sequence, not proof of the entire physical cause.

pages.title: The momentum observer, step by step
pages.section: Estimation • model residual, not a force sensor

blocks.text: The observer asks: how much of the observed momentum change cannot be explained by the model and the input we just applied? That remainder estimates external generalized force. In the present tests, ground reaction is the main external contribution; a push or model error can also appear in the residual.
p=M(q)v,\qquad \dot p=B_\tau\tau+f_p-c+\dot Mv+Q_{\mathrm{ext}}
The implemented discrete calculation

At time k, use current state, the previous state, and the input held during the completed interval. Evaluate M, bias and passive force at both endpoints. Approximate their impulse with the trapezoidal rule and include the changing-mass-matrix term:
I_k=\Delta t\left[B_\tau\tau_{k-1}+\frac{f_{p,k-1}+f_{p,k}}{2}-\frac{c_{k-1}+c_k}{2}\right]+(M_k-M_{k-1})\frac{v_{k-1}+v_k}{2}
\bar{Q}_{\mathrm{ext},k}=\frac{M_kv_k-M_{k-1}v_{k-1}-I_k}{\Delta t}

The known three motor torques are reconstructed with their modeled gains/limits. The belt surface-speed channels affect traction through contact, not through two fictitious generalized torque inputs. No direct acceleration measurement or solved contact list is read.

“No acceleration sensor” does not mean noise or model error disappears. This implementation differences estimated momentum over a finite interval, then filters it. It is a discrete momentum-residual adaptation, not a verbatim implementation of every continuous observer equation in the reference paper.

This implementation is related to generalized-momentum disturbance/residual observers. Credit De Luca and Mattone’s 2003 generalized-momenta work and 2005 collision-detection paper for the underlying idea; the floating-base discrete calculation and support interpretation are the project implementation.

pages.sources: [C7] contact_sensing.py:227–356; exact derivation and frames [A2]. Background only [T2,T3]; project equations are traced to code.

pages.title: The observer’s output has a time and a frame

blocks.text: For the six wrench rows, apply the following filter after rotating moment into the common world frame. The interval residual below denotes that frame-aligned quantity.
\hat{Q}_k=\hat{Q}_{k-1}+\alpha(\bar{Q}_{\mathrm{ext},k}-\hat{Q}_{k-1}),\qquad \alpha=1-e^{-100\Delta t}

rows: The command held from t−5 ms to t. Using the newly calculated input here would be a timing error.
An inferred average over the completed 5 ms interval, not instantaneous truth at t.
First-order memory of residuals. At Δt=5 ms, α≈0.39347 and nominal time constant=10 ms.
Separate selected normal filter:20 ms; rim treatment:200 ms. These are not the filter that directly supplies patch shares.
Computed at t, then held over the next 5 ms.

blocks.text: Frame bookkeeping

Base translation/linear velocity use world coordinates. The mirror’s free-base angular velocity uses body coordinates; Gazebo’s world angular velocity is rotated into that frame. Residual moment rows are rotated to world coordinates with a sign-consistent midpoint quaternion for the completed interval. The output is a world force F and moment m about the wheel center.

A 10 ms time constant is not a fixed 10 ms delay. At a transition, filtered force history and current geometry can combine to produce early, late or chattering patch labels. Advancing every estimate by a fixed time is not justified by that time constant.
This is 200 Hz on the simulated control clock. The saved studies did not establish a per-command real-time computation deadline.

pages.sources: [C7] _to_world/update/wrench; [C10] GazeboPlant._pull; [A2] timing/frame audit.

pages.title: From force and moment to a contact normal

blocks.text: For one ideal spherical contact, let c be the wheel center, R its radius, n the outward ground normal, and r=−Rn the center-to-contact vector. The moment about the center obeys:
m=r\times F=-R\,n\times F,\qquad p_c=c-Rn
The force and moment determine the component of n perpendicular to F. Unit length and a compressive force select the remaining component:
n_\perp=-\frac{F\times m}{R\|F\|^2}
n=\sqrt{1-\|n_\perp\|^2}\,\frac{F}{\|F\|}+n_\perp
What the code does at the limits

items: With almost zero force, the normal is undefined and the locator returns no support.

If the inferred perpendicular component is too large for a unit normal, the code normalizes that component. This keeps the output bounded; it does not prove the wrench is physically consistent with one spherical point.
Several real contacts can create one equivalent resultant. Their individual forces, identities and positions are generally not uniquely recoverable from that resultant.

blocks.text: The observer does not directly estimate “belt A.” It first estimates a net wrench. Geometry then turns that wrench into an equivalent normal/point, and a separate classifier assigns the patch. Each step can add a different kind of error.

The single-point relation assumes no independent contact couple about the point. The displayed equations explain intrinsic_normal exactly in its regular case; rim and distributed contact are handled by additional model assumptions, not by proving this single-point model universally exact.

pages.sources: [C8] contact_sensing.py:201–217,379–465; numerical/source audit [A2].

pages.title: Which shell or belt gets the load?

blocks.text: The known sphere is divided into shell bands, polar belt caps and the equatorial gap. For a current patch-axis a(q), sign s and center-to-support vector r, the locator checks a signed axial coordinate:
\xi=s\,a(q)^Tr,\qquad \xi_{\min}\leq\xi\leq\xi_{\max}

A first matching patch receives the inferred load. In the equatorial gap, two known rim points are constructed and a clipped lever rule divides their shares. The selected locator requires compressive load above 5% of model weight before returning records.
Those records have several downstream jobs

items: Patch/point/Jacobian: determine rolling rate references and belt feedforward.
Inferred load shares: blend LQR gains and route shell holding torque.
Filtered normal: changes lean and holding references; it is distinct from the raw support-share classification.
Short dropouts: the previous loaded gain/load and rolling reference can be held rather than switching abruptly to an unrelated mode.

blocks.text: Slip is estimated from velocity consistency at the inferred point. The contact estimator also maintains a friction estimate. In this selected controller, that friction estimate is diagnostic; it does not impose a hard friction-cone constraint on the final command.

A small point error need not imply correct drive assignment. If the point is only tens of micrometers from a band boundary, an equally small change can select a different input channel. Shared-rim handling is not a general arbitrary-multi-contact estimator.

pages.sources: [C8] SupportLocator and ContactEstimator; [C5] _terrain_feedback/_fade_when_unloaded; [C6] rolling branches; [A2].

pages.title: Was the robot moving during calculation?

blocks.text: The saved tests do not support that mechanism. Gazebo advances in finite blocking batches after the controller returns its command. Simulated time does not continue advancing during Python calculation between those batches.
(q_k,v_k,u_{k-1})\ \longrightarrow\ \hat F_k,\hat m_k\ \longrightarrow\ u_k\ \longrightarrow\ 5\ \mathrm{physics\ steps}

A long calculation can make the experiment slower in wall-clock time. In this lockstep execution it does not automatically mean the simulated robot has moved ahead before that command is applied. This is different from claiming computation takes zero time.
What the recordings do and do not contain

rows: Not recorded in these audited traces
An independently measured real-time delay model
Truth contact records; I-46 raw1ms substeps
Workspace inventory found no ROS .bag/.db3/.mcap recordings

blocks.text: We inspected NPZ state/command arrays and JSON/CSV/log metadata rather than assuming ROS bags exist. Aggregate run wall time cannot isolate a delayed control sample.
What can still produce a discrepancy?

items: The inferred wrench summarizes a completed interval and is filtered.
The locator evaluates that historical information at the current configuration.
Last-solver contact positions and integrated state use distinct sampling conventions.
Ideal spherical patch bands, finite collision geometry and contact tolerances differ near a boundary.

blocks.text: An estimate need not always be delayed: an estimator can be designed to estimate a current state, and a predictor can extrapolate a future state. Here the specific wrench signal is history-bearing; its patch-label error is not established as one fixed lag.

pages.sources: [C10] offroad_experiments.py:248; gazebo/plant.py:173; bridge.py:82. Read-only clock/artifact inventory [A2].

pages.title: Close point, different drive: inspect the boundary

blocks.text: At 6.855 s the interval-mean point is closer to the saved equivalent point (0.087 mm versus0.193 mm), but its patch label disagrees while the filtered label agrees. “Faster” and “closer” therefore do not automatically imply correct actuation routing.
At6.860 s, the filtered estimate is only0.183 mm away, but its selected shell upper-band margin is just0.0259 mm. That is about26 micrometers: much smaller than the point discrepancy.
The necessary qualification

At the current integrated pose, the saved true equivalent belt point itself projects about0.0782 mm outside the ideal belt band. At6.855 s it is0.0140 mm outside. Last-solver force/point, integrated pose and ideal locator geometry are not identical objects.

This confirms support-information disagreement. It does not isolate instantaneous geometric misclassification, computational latency or filter lag as the unique cause. No post-hoc clock alignment was used to eliminate the disagreement.

At6.825 s, support agrees and the belt is already over-requested. The I-42 diagnostic true-share intervention changes feedback routing but leaves the first6.860 s departure unchanged. That narrows the explanation without proving contact uncertainty is harmless.

All listed values are re-read from identical saved historical states, not newly simulated tests. “Point gap” refers to the saved load-weighted equivalent contact point and is not a claim of exact physical contact resolution.

pages.title: What prediction is actually active?
pages.section: Preview • geometric preparation, not future forces

blocks.text: The selected loop does use a small prediction: a 120 ms constant-velocity geometric preview. It advances a private configuration copy using current velocity and checks how shell/belt bands approach the estimated local plane.
q_{\mathrm{preview}}(t+h)=\operatorname{IntegratePos}(q(t),v(t)h),\qquad 0\leq h\leq0.12\ \mathrm{s}

items: For an approaching unloaded belt, request an incoming surface speed that is closer to the tangential speed at expected contact.
For an unloaded shell, form a target angular speed and bounded preparation torque. Its reaction can still affect the carrier/platform.
Preparation blend is zero for a drive carrying at least5% of current inferred normal load. Unloaded shell blend is capped at0.35.
The shell target-speed ceiling is20 rad/s. It is a preparation reference ceiling, not a general hard bound on actual shell speed.

blocks.text: What it does not compute

It does not forecast the exact future normal force, load transfer, slip, impact or changing terrain. It does not integrate the complete future closed-loop contact dynamics. It assumes the current velocity and estimated plane are useful for short-range geometric preparation.

Our present contact estimate is reactive; incoming-drive preparation is predictive in a limited geometric sense. Saying “we have no prediction” is too strong, and saying “we predict future contact forces” is also too strong.

Longer dynamic contact forecasts were evaluated as separate diagnostics and are not feeding selected live commands. The camera branch is outside this guide’s scope. The selected controller still needs current observer-based support for feedback.

pages.sources: [C9] synchronization.py:ContactSynchronizer.preview; [C5] blending and held plane; [A2].

pages.title: Why two drives can point the same way

blocks.text: A rotating joint moves a contact point along a<sub>j</sub>×r. Horizontal body motion needed for rolling is opposite that contact-surface velocity. When the shaft and loaded shell axes become geometrically aligned in their effect at contact, their two horizontal velocity vectors become parallel.
v_{xy}=D(q,r)\nu,\qquad D_j=-[a_j\times r]_{xy},\quad \nu=(\dot\theta_s,\dot\theta_h)

blocks.caption: Verified analytic reconstruction of a saved single-shell-B example. Same platform attitude, different shaft phase. Arrow columns describe motion per joint angular rate, not torque directions.

blocks.text: This is possible with ONE loaded hemisphere. It is not a consequence of “both hemispheres touching.” Tilt matters, but shaft phase, contact direction and requested travel direction also matter.

At roll−20°, pitch/yaw0°, flat normal and shaft phase−90°, both drive columns point along x. The robot can still move along x, but these two instantaneous rolling channels provide no independent y motion.

Yaw on level ground rotates the weak direction relative to a world-frame request; a pure yaw rotation does not by itself change singular values. Slope-normal and configuration changes can change the geometry itself. Instantaneous rolling authority is not a full dynamic controllability or balance certificate.

pages.title: The same attitude can have different authority

blocks.text: For the single-shell-B example, the two columns below map joint angular rates [shaft,shell B] to horizontal body rolling velocity. Entries have units meters per radian.

The matrix equations use the same roll−20° and ground normal. Only shaft phase changes. The physical singular values at−90° are approximately[0.12,0]. At−34.377°, multiplying columns by the declared5 rad/s normalization gives singular values[0.600,0.4653] m/s.

rows: Achievable kinematically with rates about(0.46985,0.17101) rad/s.
No solution using these two instantaneous rolling channels. Both columns have zero y component.

blocks.text: Near alignment, rather than perfect alignment
D=U\Sigma V^T,\qquad \nu^*=V\Sigma^{+}U^T v_{\mathrm{ref}}

A small singular value means a weak motion direction. Dividing a requested component by that small number produces a large rate demand, often with opposing drive contributions. At exactly zero, the requested component is outside the matrix’s range; a pseudoinverse cannot create it.

The correct response can include accepting motion error in the weak direction. But the body feedback reference must agree with that relaxation, and enough actuation must remain available for balance. Tilt-only weighting cannot capture all of this.

pages.section: Investigation 2 • rate demand is not torque demand

blocks.text: A different, earlier diagnostic figure-eight run contains a near-singular sample at31.650 s. It is not the6.825 s balance-demand event. Saved estimated shell-B contact and configuration give:

The damped numbers are a saved-pose algebraic comparison reconstructed from old data, not a newly actuated robot trial. The large rates are references; the torque-controlled shells would not instantly attain them.
The regularized objective explains your proposed tradeoff
\min_z\ \|D S z-v_{\mathrm{ref}}\|^2+\lambda^2\|z\|^2,\qquad \nu=S z

A positive effort weight accepts velocity mismatch instead of huge opposing rates. Bounded formulations can additionally constrain the reference. However, if LQR still tracks the original body velocity/position aggressively, it can demand large corrections downstream.
There are two distinct feasibility problems: kinematic allocation of drive rates and dynamic feasibility of balance/travel inputs. A successful fix for one is not automatically a fix for the other.

pages.title: Preparation and lean shaping change later turns
pages.section: Iteration history • evidence against one-metric tuning

blocks.caption: Saved six-turn comparisons. The interventions can improve one metric while worsening another; they do not support permanent preparation shutdown or automatic adoption of the lean shaper.

blocks.text: For example, masking preparation reduced first-turn reversal lag from1.101 to0.832 s, but introduced18.05 mm overshoot where the baseline had0. At the final listed turn, geometric overshoot increased60.20→68.41 mm. These later events occurred after the preparation intervention window ended; changed physical/controller history persisted.

Adding consistent desired tilt rate improved raw-reference lean in the demand window but increased peak belt demand relative to the angle-only arm (0.376→0.491 m/s). The arms used the same generator settings, while their closed-loop angle histories differ. The complete candidate still failed the declared raw-target attitude and turn screen. A smaller error against a newly softened target is not enough to demonstrate improved original behavior.
What is known about the cause?

items: Confirmed: response is delayed at some reversals; real geometric overshoot occurs at others; problems appear on flat as well as Mars cases.
Confirmed: reference, balance feedback, preparation reactions and carried history affect the outcome.

Not isolated: a unique term or one tuning value that explains and fixes all turns. Saturation and weak rolling directions can contribute, but the saved turn evidence alone does not prove they cause each overshoot.

blocks.text: The current LQR baseline was retained. We should explain that decision as a result of measured nonregression criteria, not as a claim that every trial failed in every way.

pages.title: What the investigation supports next
pages.section: Proposed • no implementation in this task

blocks.text: Prioritize constraint-consistent reference/control design and measured turn response. Do not assume a faster contact filter or a larger effort weight is the missing universal fix.
1. Keep identifying which part hits the limit

For each saved correction, align body/reference attitude and rate, per-term LQR contributions, rolling/holding/preparation additions, requested versus applied input, contact margins and turning metrics. The6.825 s and31.650 s examples must remain distinct mechanisms.
2. Make relaxation consistent across the loop

If motion along a weak direction is intentionally reduced, update the body velocity/position feedback reference consistently. Check the total balance-plus-travel command, not only kinematic rate references. Retain meaningful balance priority; record infeasibility rather than promising every requested motion can be performed.
3. A candidate must add something beyond clipping

A reference governor or an explicitly constrained local model can be investigated while retaining LQR as the nominal feedback. A purely box-constrained projection of the requested input may reproduce today’s clipping. Dynamic/geometry-aware constraints or priorities are needed to change the feasibility decision meaningfully.
4. Treat contact ambiguity as an uncertainty signal

Near a patch edge, report margin and support disagreement. The current observer cannot uniquely recover arbitrary simultaneous contacts. Any future handoff rule should be checked against both early and late transitions, existing gain blending/preparation and the correct time convention.
5. Require multiple objectives to pass together

A later candidate should be compared on saturation, raw/reference-relative attitude, original-path error, turn overshoot/lag, settling and completion. Preserve regressions. The present task deliberately stops at saved-data diagnosis and the study guide.

These are proposed design directions, not a stability proof, validated controller or an instruction to rerun simulations. The prior bounded/feasible/tilt trials remain relevant negative evidence that a simplistic repeat is insufficient.

pages.title: Practice: control and constraint questions
pages.section: Professor Q&A • answer, then point to evidence

blocks.text: Why does LQR exceed limits if we penalize effort?

Because a finite cost discourages input; it does not impose |u|≤b. In this implementation the Riccati problem is unconstrained. The issued input is bounded later by clipping, which does not make the requested state transition feasible.
So is the controller broken?

The clipping mechanism is working as specified. The design is incomplete with respect to constrained closed-loop feasibility and balance/tracking priorities. We have identified that gap; we have not solved it or proved it is the only cause of every deviation.
Why not just raise the effort weight?

It can reduce input demand while increasing response lag or balance error. Earlier damping/weight trials show those tradeoffs. Also, a rate-allocation cost cannot directly fix a large LQR balance term; inspect the contribution first.
Does bounded allocation constrain the complete controller?

No. It constrains selected drive-rate references under its assumptions. The downstream feedback, holding and preparation contributions can still request more input. Actual joint speed is a dynamic state, not the same thing as a capped rate reference.
Are you optimizing torque or speed?

Both kinds of channels appear, but at different stages: actual inputs are three torques and two belt surface speeds; the rolling allocator computes three angular-rate references plus two surface-speed references. Their normalized costs are not motor power.
Is the LQR globally stable?

No such claim is established. Local design/eigenvalue checks do not certify nonlinear contact switches, gain interpolation, estimation errors, friction and saturation. Successful selected trials are empirical evidence, not a global proof.
Why can small desired body speed require large belt speed?

A local surface speed is not body translation. At6.825 s the body target is about0.045 m/s, but the LQR requests substantial belt motion to correct attitude and angular rate. At31.650 s a separate weak-geometry mechanism produces extreme joint-rate references.

pages.sources: Answers are supported by the saved decomposition and source/log audits [A1,A3], not an assumed new controller.

pages.title: Practice: estimation, prediction and evidence
pages.section: Professor Q&A • use the correct clock

blocks.text: Does the momentum observer read contact truth?

Not in the selected observer-and-locator loop. It reads current/prior configuration and velocity, known prior applied commands and model terms. The separate evaluator reads solved contacts. Exact simulated body state is supplied; that assumption must be stated.
Is the contact point old because the calculation takes time?

The wrench is history-bearing, but simulated physics does not advance between finite lockstep runs. These logs do not measure CPU/transport delay as the cause. We should separately discuss filtering, completed-interval information and geometry at current pose.
Why can a close contact point select the wrong motor?

Identity is a discrete band decision. The point error can be larger than its tiny boundary margin. Also, last-solver truth and current integrated pose need not lie on exactly the same ideal band. The6.860 s sample demonstrates disagreement, not a uniquely isolated latency mechanism.
Are we predicting contact?

The support estimate is reactive. The active synchronizer predicts geometric exposure up to120 ms under constant velocity on the estimated plane. It prepares drives; it does not predict exact future forces or guarantee a handoff.
Would perfect contact solve the tracking problem?

Not demonstrated. The I-42 diagnostic true-share substitution changes routing without preventing the first departure. At an earlier inspected instant both assignments agree while the belt is already over-requested.
Can the observer resolve several independent contacts?

Not generally from one net wrench. The implementation returns an equivalent spherical support and has a specific two-rim lever model. Those assumptions do not identify every possible simultaneous contact distribution.
What did the latest contact-filter test actually improve?

Some historical labels and one fresh transition improved, but paired median timing benefit was0 ms and maximum command jumps were unchanged. The faster variant was shadow-only; we did not demonstrate a different driving trajectory.

blocks.text: The nominal18-component error layout is below. The design normalizes each group, applies the listed Q weights and transforms the result back to physical units. The running controller then deliberately modifies selected error entries as explained earlier.

The input normalization uses bounds[1.5,0.6,0.6,0.3,0.3]; R<sub>u</sub>=diag(0.3,0.3,0.3,1,1). Selected gains use the full18-coordinate nominal design followed by reachable-subspace reduction. An optional frozen_phase=True comparison branch omits selected yaw/material-angle coordinates; it is not active here. Runtime suppresses or changes selected errors separately, while logging all18 entries.
Six definitions worth being able to say

items: Jacobian: maps a small joint/base velocity into contact-point velocity; its transpose maps a contact force into generalized force.
Feedforward: input/reference contribution computed from the desired motion or holding model, before observing the resulting tracking error.
Feedback: correction based on current error relative to the chosen reference.
Observer: uses measurements plus a model to estimate an unmeasured quantity.
Singular value: measures gain along a particular independent input/output direction; a small value indicates weak instantaneous authority.
Constraint versus cost: a constraint restricts the allowed set; a cost ranks choices inside the optimization’s allowed set.

blocks.text: Study test: explain why a cap on a rate reference does not guarantee a torque bound, why torque clipping does not guarantee tracking, and why a small point error does not guarantee the correct support label.
